## Proof

Let $(Y_n)_{n \geq 1}$ be independent random variables, each exponentially distributed with parameter $\lambda = 2$, so that
$$P(Y_n > y) = e^{-2y}, \quad y \geq 0.$$

We determine the almost-sure value of
$$L := \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{Y_n}{\log(n+1)}.$$

---

**Upper bound: $L \leq \tfrac{1}{2}$ a.s.**

Fix any $c > \tfrac{1}{2}$. Then
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P\!\left(Y_n > c\,\log(n+1)\right) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} e^{-2c\,\log(n+1)} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (n+1)^{-2c}.$$

Since $2c > 1$, this $p$-series converges. By the **first Borel–Cantelli lemma**,
$$P\!\left(Y_n > c\,\log(n+1) \text{ infinitely often}\right) = 0.$$

Hence, with probability $1$, only finitely many of the events $\{Y_n > c\log(n+1)\}$ occur, which gives
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{Y_n}{\log(n+1)} \leq c \quad \text{a.s.}$$

Taking a countable intersection over $c = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{k}$, $k = 1, 2, \dots$,
$$L \leq \tfrac{1}{2} \quad \text{a.s.}$$

---

**Lower bound: $L \geq \tfrac{1}{2}$ a.s.**

Fix any $c < \tfrac{1}{2}$. Then $2c < 1$, so
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P\!\left(Y_n > c\,\log(n+1)\right) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (n+1)^{-2c} = \infty.$$

Since the $Y_n$ are **independent**, the events $\{Y_n > c\log(n+1)\}$ are independent. By the **second Borel–Cantelli lemma**,
$$P\!\left(Y_n > c\,\log(n+1) \text{ infinitely often}\right) = 1.$$

Therefore
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{Y_n}{\log(n+1)} \geq c \quad \text{a.s.}$$

Taking a countable intersection over $c = \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{k}$, $k = 1, 2, \dots$,
$$L \geq \tfrac{1}{2} \quad \text{a.s.}$$

---

**Conclusion.**

Combining the upper and lower bounds,
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{Y_n}{\log(n+1)} = \frac{1}{2} \quad \text{almost surely.}$$

Therefore
$$\boxed{P\!\left(\limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{Y_n}{\log(n+1)} = \frac{1}{2}\right) = 1.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
